introduction: On this Sunday, Wisdom prepares a banquet and invites the simple to come and eat her bread and drink her wine. In the Gospel, Jesus says, My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed; whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. Paul urges us to be filled with the Spirit and to give thanks always. Let us receive the Eucharist with faith and thanksgiving.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, let us taste and see the goodness of the Lord, and bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may always be nourished by the Body and Blood of Christ. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those preparing for First Communion: that they may come to the table of the Lord with faith and joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are hungry for bread or for meaning: that they may be fed. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who doubt the presence of Christ in the Eucharist: that the Lord may give them faith. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may be filled with the Spirit and give thanks always for all things. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your Son gives us his flesh as food and his blood as drink. May we who receive him live in him and he in us, now and forever. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Food indeed
reflection.body:
In the first reading, Wisdom is pictured as a gracious hostess who has "built her house" and prepared a feast. She sends out her servants with an invitation to the simple: "Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!" And she promises: "Leave your simple ways, and live." Christians have long seen in this banquet an image of the Eucharist, where Christ, the Wisdom of God, feeds his people.

In the Gospel, Jesus continues his teaching on the bread of life. He says plainly: "the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh." His listeners are shocked: "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" Jesus does not soften his words. He repeats them even more strongly: "unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don't have life in yourselves."

And again: "For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed." The Church believes that in the Eucharist we truly receive the Body and Blood of Christ. This is not a symbol only, but Christ himself, giving himself to us as food.

Jesus explains what this communion does: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him." Communion is a bond of life with Jesus. And it is a promise of the future: "He who eats this bread will live forever."

Paul tells the Ephesians how to live this out: "be filled with the Spirit," singing to the Lord and "giving thanks always concerning all things." The word Eucharist itself means thanksgiving.

This week, prepare for Communion with a moment of silence before Mass. After receiving, stay a moment and speak to Jesus who lives in you. And give thanks for one thing each day.
